result.title: Preface
result.summary: KCERA’s Request for Proposal for audit services outlines the engagement, including general information, term, and auditor qualifications; the retirement system’s background, investments, accounting, systems, expenses, actuarial information, benefits, reserves, and records; required audit scope, standards, and working-paper access and retention; required reports and communications, including irregularities, illegal acts, and compliance; schedule, final-report deadline for the 2019–20 audit, and inquiries; assistance and entrance, progress, and exit conferences. It also specifies proposal preparation, submission, withdrawal, communications, required contents and sealed cost bid; evaluation and selection procedures; rejection rights, public-record disclosure, conflicts and collusion; and contract form. Exhibits include California retirement-system minimum audit and reporting guidelines and a sample audit-services agreement.

result.title: KCERA REQUEST FOR PROPOSAL – AUDIT SERVICES
result.summary: KCERA solicits CPA proposals to audit its financial statements for FY 2022–23 and the following two years, under Government Auditing Standards and California State Controller requirements. The engagement may be extended up to three years; KCERA staff and its Finance Committee evaluate proposals for Board selection. The RFP describes KCERA’s governance, membership, investments, accounting and pension systems, budget and expense limits, actuarial valuations and assumptions, benefit provisions, and reserve rules. Auditors must meet public-pension and California licensing qualifications. Work includes a GAAP financial-statement opinion, required supplementary-information procedures, ACFR review, internal-control and compliance reporting, communications, and census-data sampling; a separately priced AU-C 805 opinion on GASB 68 schedules is also requested. Proposals must address firm independence, qualifications, staffing, references, relevant experience, access to other entities, methodology, work plan, hours, and schedule. The RFP sets proposal, audit, reporting, and communication deadlines; working-paper retention and access rules; submission requirements, costs, and KCERA’s rights to reject or waive defects.

nodes.title: A. General Information
nodes.summary: KCERA seeks proposals from qualified CPA firms to audit its financial statements for the fiscal year ending June 30, 2023, and the following two fiscal years. Audits must follow U.S. Government Auditing Standards and California State Controller requirements for public retirement systems. Questions must be emailed to matt.henry@kcera.org; proposals are due March 3, 2023, at 2:00 p.m. PST, and KCERA may reject any submission. KCERA staff will evaluate proposals and submit ratings and recommendations to the Finance Committee, comprising four retirement trustees and an alternate; the committee will recommend a firm to the Board of Retirement. KCERA will prepare the resulting agreement, with a sample provided as Exhibit B. Any objections to its terms must be explained in a separate letter included with the proposal.

nodes.title: B. Term of Engagement
nodes.summary:
B. Term of Engagement
A three-year agreement is contemplated, subject to the annual review and recommendation of the Board of Retirement and the satisfactory negotiation of terms, including a price acceptable to both KCERA and the selected firm. The term of the original agreement may be extended for up to an additional three years upon the mutual agreement of KCERA and the selected firm.

nodes.title: C. Qualification of the Auditor
nodes.summary: Auditors must meet State Controller standards for auditing, government accounting, pension accounting and actuarial knowledge; a senior engagement-team member must be California-licensed as a CPA or registered public accountant. KCERA is a 1945 cost-sharing defined-benefit pension plan for Kern County and 14 participating agencies, serving about 9,076 active and 13,030 retired/deferred members, with $5.1 billion in assets at June 30, 2022. It holds contributions and investment income as fiduciary, and is governed by a nine-member Board and three alternates; the Board and staff administer benefits, services, accounting, systems and investments, with 35 budgeted positions in FY 2021–22. The Board oversees external investment managers, supported by consultants, an Investment Committee and Deutsche Bank securities lending; the CIO oversees but does not internally manage investments. KCERA follows GASB standards and prepares an ACFR intended to meet GFOA award requirements. Systems include a LAN, Great Plains accounting, County FMS/voucher and payroll services, and CPAS for pension administration and benefit payments. The Board adopts the annual operating budget; expenses are charged to fund earnings and capped at 0.21% of actuarial accrued liability, while capital assets are depreciated over useful lives. Segal Consulting performs annual valuations and triennial assumption reviews under California law.

nodes.title: KCERA Systems and Administrative Expenses
nodes.summary: The page references the Government Finance Officers Association’s Certificate of Achievement for Excellence in Financial Reporting. KCERA’s systems include a LAN; Microsoft Dynamics Great Plains for accounting and financial statements; Kern County’s FMS and Voucher Program for administrative and investment expense payments; county-paid employee payroll; and CPAS for pension administration, including importing active-member biweekly payroll and processing benefit payments for bank transfer. The Board of Retirement adopts KCERA’s operating budget annually. Administrative expenses are charged to fund earnings under CERL and capped at 0.21% of actuarial accrued liability. Budgeted capital assets are capitalized when purchased and expensed over their useful lives.

nodes.title: F. Actuarial Services and Information
nodes.summary:
F. Actuarial Services and Information
KCERA engages an independent actuarial firm, Segal Consulting, to conduct annual actuarial valuations to monitor KCERA’s funding status. On a triennial basis, these valuations are updated for economic and non-economic assumptions as required by the California Government Code. The triennial
KCERA Request for Proposal – Audit Services
Page 4valuation was performed as of June 30, 2019. The June 30, 2022 valuation determined KCERA’s funded ratio to be 69.2%.
Both the triennial and annual valuations use the entry age normal method, and an actuarial 5-year smoothing of asset values. The current valuation uses a 7.25% interest assumption and a 3.25% salary assumption.

nodes.title: G. Benefit Provisions
nodes.summary: KCERA provides retirement, disability, death, beneficiary, cost-of-living, and supplemental retirement benefits, and all eligible employees must participate. Members may retire at age 50 with 10 years of service, or regardless of age with 30 years for general members or 20 years for safety members. Monthly benefits depend on final monthly compensation, retirement age, and service years. Retirees and continuance beneficiaries receive annual COLA adjustments of up to 2.5%. Members leaving County service may withdraw their contributions plus interest. Members leaving after at least five years may keep contributions on deposit and, once vested, qualify for deferred benefits upon reaching age 50 with at least 10 years of system participation. Those entering a reciprocal retirement system within six months may leave contributions with KCERA and establish reciprocity regardless of KCERA service length. Reciprocal systems include qualifying 1937 Act counties, CalPERS, and California public agencies with CalPERS reciprocity agreements.

nodes.title: H. Reserves
key_items: 1. Other Services Required – GASB Statement No. 68 Schedules
nodes.summary: Effective July 1, 1984, Kern County adopted CERL Article 5.5, establishing alternative provisions for reserves, earnings and surplus, benefit and function costs, retiree benefits, cost-of-living adjustments, contingency reserves, transfers and distributions, actuarial-rate and net-earnings definitions and crediting, and certain retirement-board recommendations. A 2001 resolution requires part of cost-of-living contributions to come from excess interest earnings. KCERA seeks qualified CPA firms to audit its financial statements for the engagement term, opine on GAAP presentation, perform required procedures on supplementary information, review internal controls, accounting policies and GAAP compliance, and review the ACFR. Supporting schedules are unaudited but receive an in-relation-to opinion; introductory, investment, actuarial and statistical sections are checked for consistency. Auditors sample pension-system census and member data. Additional work requires a separate proposal and fee, and KCERA may select another provider. A separate bid is requested for AU-C 805 opinions on GASB 68 schedules, including specified employer-allocation and pension-amount totals, plus required employer-auditor communications and census-data testing.

nodes.title: C. Auditing Standards to be Followed
nodes.summary:
C. Auditing Standards to be Followed
To meet the requirements of this RFP, the audit shall be performed in accordance with Government Auditing Standards, as set forth by the Comptroller General of the United States, and with the “Minimum Audit Requirements and Reporting Guidelines for California Public Retirement Systems” issued by the California State Controller. (See Exhibit A.)

nodes.title: D. Working Paper Retention and Access to Working Papers
nodes.summary: Auditors must retain working papers at their expense during the engagement and at least five years afterward, unless KCERA extends or permits earlier disposal; provide them to KCERA on request and cooperate with successor auditors. Required deliverables include annual GAAP financial-statement opinions, reporting on legal noncompliance, communications to the Board on audit responsibilities, policies, estimates, adjustments, disagreements, prior discussions, difficulties and findings, immediate written notice of irregularities or suspected illegal acts, and Government Auditing Standards reports on compliance and internal-control scope and significant deficiencies. The RFP timeline runs January–March 2023, with contract award planned for April 12. The 2022–23 draft is due in October, with review and possible November meetings; final signed reports are due in early December, electronically and in two originals. Questions go by email by February 10, with answers posted by February 17; KCERA may waive minor defects. KCERA prepares financial materials and provides workspace. Auditors attend entrance/exit conferences and provide at least weekly progress reports. Proposals are emailed by March 3 at 2 p.m.; rules cover costs, rejection, formatting, withdrawal, 90-day validity, and restricted contact with KCERA personnel.

nodes.title: E. Proposal Contents
nodes.summary: Proposals must follow the specified order and label six sections: Cover Letter, Table of Contents, Executive Summary, Technical Proposal, sealed dollar cost bid, and additional data/attachments. The one-page cover letter identifies the firm and structure, audit-office contact details, KCERA liaison and contract-authorized representative, and proposal date. The contents list sections, subsections, and page numbers. The executive summary states understanding, timely-performance commitment, qualifications, and that the offer is irrevocable for 90 days. The technical proposal describes capabilities and covers independence; California licensure and required certifications; firm size, staffing, regulatory matters and litigation; assigned personnel’s qualifications, experience, training, memberships, continuity, and replacement approvals; similar recent engagements and client references; access to relevant government or other entities; and the audit approach. The approach explains requirements, methodology, work plan, proposed engagement segments, staffing levels and hours, and any clearly identified additional services, priced separately in the sealed bid.

For the Respondent’s firm that will be assigned responsibility for the audit, list the most significant engagements performed in the last four (4) years that are similar to the engagement described in this RFP. First list prior engagements auditing public retirement systems and then engagements with Kern County or other government agencies. g. Liaison with other entities
The Respondent should describe arrangements that it has with regard to liaison with or access to offices of the state and federal governments or other entities relevant to this engagement for the purpose of obtaining prompt responses to inquiries arising from technical or procedural questions developed in the course of the examination.

nodes.title: h. Specific audit approach
nodes.summary: The proposal must explain the respondent’s understanding of the engagement, work plan, and audit methodology for services in RFP Sections III–V. It may include additional services deemed necessary, which must be clearly identified and priced separately in the sealed cost bid (Attachment 3). The response must describe engagement segments; staffing levels and estimated hours for each; compliance with Section V timing requirements; analytical procedures; supervisory review and direction; how the respondent will understand and document KCERA’s internal controls; and how applicable laws and regulations will be identified for audit testing.

result.title: i. Procedures for resolving potential audit problems
result.summary: The proposal must explain how the respondent will address potential audit problems and any special assistance it may request from KCERA. The sealed dollar cost bid (Attachment 3) must include all pricing for the requested audit. Its first page must identify the firm, certify the signer’s authority to represent the firm, submit the bid, and sign a KCERA contract, and state separate not-to-exceed costs for the independent financial statement audit and GAS 68 schedules. The maximum price must include all direct and indirect costs, including out-of-pocket expenses. Proposal and bid preparation and submission costs are the respondent’s responsibility and must not be included.

result.title: b. Rates by staff classification and anticipated hours
result.summary: Bids must provide professional-fee and expense schedules by audit year, anticipated staff classification and hours, and any additional services; estimated reimbursable expenses count toward the not-to-exceed price. KCERA-requested supplemental services require an addendum and use bid rates. Progress payments are billed at least monthly for completed work and approved expenses, with 10% withheld until final reports. KCERA evaluates compliant proposals based on independence, licensure, conflicts, approach, deliverables, schedule, staffing, firm and personnel qualifications, and cost, which is not the primary factor. Staff, the Finance Committee, and the Board review and recommend or select a firm; KCERA negotiates fees, may approach the next-ranked firm, and may conduct background inquiries. KCERA retains discretion to reject proposals, waive minor irregularities, seek clarification, and disqualify misrepresentation or improper influence. Proposals are public records; confidentiality claims, disclosure risks, indemnity, and conflict certifications apply. The RFP includes a sample contract; unchallenged terms are accepted, while requested changes must be itemized and justified, and late negotiations may be ended.

nodes.title: Audit Fees, Expenses, and Additional Services
key_items: c. Out-of-pocket expenses included in the total not-to-exceed maximum price and reimbursement rates
d. Rates for additional professional services
nodes.summary: The sealed cost bid should include professional fee and expense schedules supporting the total not-to-exceed price, with separate schedules for each audit year and, if needed, additional services. Estimated reimbursable out-of-pocket expenses must be disclosed and count toward that price. Additional services requested by KCERA to supplement the RFP or address report recommendations require an agreement addendum and will use the rates in the bid’s fee and expense schedule.

nodes.title: e. Manner of Payment
nodes.summary: Progress payments are based on completed work hours and approved out-of-pocket expenses, billed at least monthly; 10% is withheld until final reports are delivered. Respondents may include optional additional data, such as promotional brochures with minimal technical content and pictorial materials. KCERA may evaluate any relevant factors. Staff review proposals and recommend to the Finance Committee, which recommends to the Board; employees with disqualifying relationships cannot participate, and respondents must disclose such relationships. Proposals undergo a three-step review: staff ranking of compliant proposals, Finance Committee review and recommendation, then Board consideration. Criteria include independence and California licensure, conflicts, RFP compliance, audit plans and approach, deliverables, schedule, staffing and supervision, firm experience, capabilities and stability, personnel qualifications and continuing education, and cost (hours, rates, maximum price, and annual-audit flat fee); cost is not primary. KCERA negotiates fees with the preferred firm, may approach the next-ranked firm if negotiations fail, and may conduct background inquiries, with respondent consent and access to requested records. The Finance Committee is expected to recommend a firm for Board contract award at its subsequent meeting.

nodes.title: f. Evaluation Criteria
nodes.summary: KCERA has sole discretion over RFP evaluation procedures and recommendations, provided selections are not arbitrary or capricious and have a reasonable basis. It may reject any or all proposals, waive minor irregularities, deem missing information nonresponsive, reject or retain proposals with errors, and request clarification. Misrepresentation, omission, or attempts to obtain an improper advantage through third parties disqualify respondents. Proposals become KCERA property and are subject to California Public Records Act disclosure; recommended proposals may also appear on public agendas. Respondents may mark specific portions confidential, but KCERA decides whether they are exempt and may notify respondents to seek a protective order. Respondents must indemnify KCERA for claims related to withholding or disclosing marked material and include a specified indemnity clause when submitting confidential or proprietary information. KCERA discourages such information, and submission waives claims arising from proposal inspection. Respondents certify prices are genuine and that they have no actual or potential conflicts preventing service in KCERA’s best interests.

nodes.title: SECTION XI. CONTRACT FORM
nodes.summary: The RFP includes a sample audit-services agreement as Exhibit B. Proposals that do not comment on it are deemed to accept all terms without seeking changes. Any objections or requests to modify or add terms must identify each item, provide proposed language, and explain the reasons. KCERA may consider proposed changes during selection and may revise the contract before execution. To avoid delays from extended negotiations, KCERA may end negotiations with the selected respondent if amendment requests are made after the finalist interview or during negotiations.

result.title: QUALIFICATIONS AND EXPERIENCE CERTIFICATION
result.summary: Attachment 1 of KCERA’s audit-services RFP requires bidders to certify qualifications and experience by providing relevant firm qualifications and supporting information, the firm’s California State Board of Accountancy license, and resumes for the engagement partner, manager, and senior/on-site supervisor, including retirement-system audit experience. Proposed team members may not be replaced without KCERA’s prior approval; substitute resumes and required certifications must accompany the change request. CPA-license copies are required for the engagement partner, manager, and on-site supervisor: the senior must hold a California State Board of Accountancy license, while the manager and on-site supervisor may hold licenses from any U.S. state. The response must be signed by an authorized firm representative and include their title, printed name, and date.

result.title: MINIMUM AND DESIRABLE QUALIFICATIONS CERTIFICATION
result.summary: The attachment is a yes/no certification of minimum and desirable qualifications for KCERA audit services. Minimum qualifications require a U.S.-based professional public accounting firm with regional organization and audit/attest services; firms’ five-year history includes merged or acquired entities. The firm must have completed at least five audits in the past five years of defined-benefit plans with assets over $2 billion, experience auditing domestic and foreign equities, fixed income, real estate, alternatives, commodities and securities lending, and a U.S. office. It must be independent and licensed and in good standing in California. The U.S.-based engagement partner/signing partner must be a California CPA with 10+ years’ public-accounting experience including pension audits; the U.S.-based manager must have five-plus years and the supervisor three-plus years of relevant experience and CPA licensure. Manager and supervisor must be available year-round. Desirable qualifications include no specified litigation or professional-regulatory proceedings; partner and manager each having two recent audits of plans over $3 billion; California licensure for the manager; and no specified investigations or proceedings affecting the firm’s ability to perform, with information kept confidential until public unless law requires otherwise.

result.title: BACKGROUND AND REFERENCE CHECKS
result.summary: Attachment 4 of the Kern County Employees’ Retirement Association audit-services RFP requires bidders to provide at least three business references familiar with the firm’s work from the past five years. At least two references must be qualifying defined-benefit pension plans; two years auditing the same plan satisfies this requirement. The reference form requests the company name and address, contact person, telephone and fax numbers, email address, and a description of services provided. The text also identifies Exhibit A: the California State Controller’s minimum audit requirements and reporting guidelines for public retirement systems.

result.title: INTRODUCTION
result.summary: The exhibit sets minimum—not comprehensive—audit requirements prescribed by the State Controller under Government Code Sections 7501–7504. Auditors of public retirement systems should be trained in generally accepted auditing standards and knowledgeable about government accounting, pension accounting, and actuarial science. Audits must follow generally accepted standards and consider evaluating internal controls and financial organization to guide audit testing; obtaining sufficient evidence through inspection, observation, inquiries, and confirmations, with control deficiencies explained and opinions qualified where appropriate; reviewing applicable regulations and referring suspected violations to legal counsel, reporting confirmed noncompliance and qualifying or disclaiming the opinion as needed; and checking that financial transaction reports filed with the State Controller agree with the system’s official records.

result.title: MINIMUM AUDIT REQUIREMENTS
result.summary: Auditors should review prior audit workpapers and programs; identify the accounting basis, using accrual accounting for a fair, fully disclosed financial position; confirm bank and savings accounts and related collateral, and assess collateral’s adequacy and propriety; test the recording of ascertainable revenues; verify that expenditures are authorized and documented; review the legality and recording of nonrevenue receipts and non-expense disbursements; verify other assets and liabilities under generally accepted auditing standards; and contact appropriate authorities about possible contingent liabilities.

result.title: AUDIT REPORT REQUIREMENTS
result.summary: Exhibit A specifies audit report requirements: state whether financial statements follow generally accepted accounting principles and whether those principles were applied consistently with the preceding period; include footnote disclosures and supplementary information required by GASB Statement 25; and provide a fairness opinion under State Board of Accountancy Rules 58.1 and 58.21, which may be unqualified, qualified, adverse, or a disclaimer. The report must use fair value as described in GASB Statement 25 and separately disclose net appreciation or depreciation in investment fair value. A suggested report format includes a title page, table of contents, and sections for scope, opinion, and other necessary paragraphs. The text cites 16 Cal. Adm. Code 58.1–58.2.

result.title: EXCERPTS FROM THE CALIFORNIA GOVERNMENT CODE RELATING TO PUBLIC RETIREMENT SYSTEM REPORTS TO THE STATE CONTROLLER
result.summary: The provisions aim to protect public retirement systems’ solvency through independent financial analysis and comparable reporting. The State Controller reviews annual reports, emphasizing funding adequacy, and triennial valuations, examining key actuarial assumptions; an advisory committee of enrolled actuaries and system administrators assists. Systems must prepare annual GAAP reports and, at least every three years, obtain a valuation from an experienced enrolled actuary using agency-established assumptions, disclosing significant differences and their effects. They must also obtain an attest audit by an authorized CPA, public accountant, or specified county auditor, and submit GAAP audited statements in the Controller’s prescribed form within six months after each fiscal year. The Controller publishes an annual report and may waive late-filing penalties for good cause. Local agencies may establish pension trusts using authorized insurance, annuity, or other investments; participation may be optional or compulsory, with contributions deducted from compensation. Officials who fail to file after notice face revenue-based forfeitures of $1,000, $2,500, or $5,000, prosecuted by the Attorney General upon the Controller’s request.

result.title: W I T N E S S E T H:
result.summary: The agreement sets requirements for KCERA’s annual financial and compliance audits, including internal-control testing, ACFR and schedule review, accounting advice, and reporting under applicable standards and guidelines. It establishes meetings and presentations, prompt reporting of suspected misuse or serious noncompliance, and KCERA’s duty to provide records and assistance. It covers fees, invoicing, withholding, term, termination, deadlines and extensions, and prior written approval for assignment. The Auditor warrants its qualifications and performance, serves as an independent contractor, indemnifies KCERA for negligence and errors or omissions, and must carry specified insurance. Other provisions address work papers, confidentiality and public records, personnel, notices, conflicts, authority, amendments, governing law and venue, remedies, severability, legal compliance, recordkeeping and audit access, nondiscrimination, non-collusion, interpretation, execution, and no third-party rights.

nodes.title: WHEREAS:
nodes.summary: The agreement requires KCERA’s annual financial and compliance audits under applicable law, including internal-control testing, review of the ACFR and supporting schedules, accounting-policy advice, and reporting under Government Auditing Standards and state guidelines. The Auditor must meet with staff or committees regarding material issues, present results to the Board and requested committees, and promptly report suspected fund misuse or serious noncompliance. KCERA will provide records, confirmations, explanations, and review assistance. Compensation, invoicing, withholding, term, termination, audit deadlines and qualifying extensions are specified; assignment needs written approval. The Auditor warrants qualifications and timely professional performance, acts as an independent contractor, indemnifies KCERA for negligence and errors or omissions, and must maintain required liability, workers’ compensation, and professional-liability insurance. General provisions address work-paper ownership, confidentiality and public records, personnel changes, notices, conflicts, authority, amendments, governing law and venue, remedies, severability, compliance, records and audit access, nondiscrimination, non-collusion, interpretation, execution, and absence of third-party rights.

nodes.title: WHEREAS: (intro)
nodes.summary: The agreement states that KCERA must obtain annual financial audits under Government Code sections 7504(b) and 31593, and seeks a compliance audit of its administration’s internal controls to help safeguard assets and ensure compliance with laws and Board policies. After evaluating qualified firms, KCERA selected the Auditor, which represents that it is trained, licensed, experienced, and qualified. The Auditor will annually conduct independent financial and compliance audits, test accounting records and other necessary procedures, and report whether the financial statements are fairly presented under Government Auditing Standards and California State Controller guidelines, with further details incorporated by reference to an exhibit. The Auditor must arrange special meetings with staff or the Finance Committee when fieldwork identifies a potentially material issue; attend at least one Board meeting annually to present results and at least two Committee meetings when requested by the CEO; and immediately report suspected or actual fund defalcation or misuse, and serious legal or regulatory noncompliance, in writing to the Board Chair and CEO.

nodes.title: E. Auditor shall review and test the KCERA’s internal controls in as complete
nodes.summary: The agreement requires the Auditor to test KCERA’s internal controls, review the ACFR and supporting schedules, and advise on accounting policies. KCERA must explain audit requirements, provide confirmations and requested records, meet to discuss controls, review draft reports promptly, and assist as specified. Compensation follows an inserted schedule and cap, with no separate overhead or clerical charges; approved itemized invoices are paid within 30 days, with 10% withheld until Board approval of the final report. The agreement has specified start and end dates and either party may terminate on 30 days’ notice. The Auditor warrants adequate expertise, no adverse interests, and timely professional performance. Audit deadlines run from September fieldwork through the November Board report; qualifying delays extend deadlines without damages or extra compensation. Assignment requires written approval. The Auditor is an independent contractor and bears employment obligations. The Auditor must indemnify KCERA for negligence and errors or omissions, perform to professional standards, and maintain workers’ compensation, general liability (at least $1 million per occurrence/$5 million aggregate), and auto liability (at least $1 million per occurrence) insurance.

nodes.title: D. Professional Liability (Errors and Omissions) Insurance, for liability arising
nodes.summary: Requires professional-liability insurance of at least $5 million per claim, full prior acts for claims-made policies, insurers rated at least A-,VII, continuous coverage, advance cancellation/material-change notice, annual certificates, specified additional-insured status, and policy/financial-statement copies on request. Coverage is primary and does not limit liability; failure to maintain it is a material breach. General terms require professional care, notice before changing lead personnel, KCERA ownership of work papers, protection of sensitive information subject to public-records laws, and independent-contractor status. Notices, conflict-of-interest obligations, the entire-agreement rule, limits on auditor authority, written-only amendments, nonwaiver, California law and Kern County venue are specified. Remedies are cumulative; provisions address severability, legal compliance, interpretation, time being of the essence (with delay exceptions), counterparts, nondiscrimination, recordkeeping and audit access for at least three years, non-collusion, signing authority, and no third-party rights. The agreement includes execution and approval signature blocks.
